# Progress log

## dosunit differential sweep — full coverage milestone

Final state after the fixture-hardening work:

- **311 ported routines: 0 diff, 0 uncovered**
- 76 dedicated specs + 212 probe-agree + 5 probe-mix + 11 artifact +
  7 incomplete + 0 skipped
- Dedicated suites (~1700 vectors): all AGREE — egame_tac 341,
  egame_combat 209, egame_state 269, egame_state2 226, edge 36,
  start_math 157, egame_scalelod 147, egame_math2 72, start_util 151,
  plus clock/objective/bufpos/select/wrap/su_wrap shards.

### Fixture layers (all in `dosunit/gen_probe.py` + `tools/duspec.py`)

| layer | mechanism |
|---|---|
| slotstub | every oracle driver-ABI `EA` slot -> `xor ax,ax; retf` |
| int_stub | reachable `CD xx` -> `xor ax,ax` (BFS over call/lcall/jmp graph) |
| int_stub_c | same for the candidate image |
| call_stub | oracle calls into cand-side trivial stubs -> nop/`pop ax`/`xor ax,ax` |
| dsss_stub | reachable `ds:=ss` writes nopped (DS==SS under DOS) |
| reloc-drop | MZ relocs overlapping any patched span are removed |

Key invariants learned:

- `_drop_relocs_overlapping` is mandatory on every patched span — the MZ
  loader rewrites relocated words inside nop'd `9A` lcalls and desyncs the
  instruction stream (`90 90` -> `90 a0`).
- `stub_models` peels leading casts — `return (int16)a;` classifies as a
  param-return stub (`sub_15AD2` callers `sub_15460`/`sub_15B68`/
  `setViewOrigin` were unpatched until then).
- `sub_<linaddr>` stub names index linear image offsets; 5-digit hex
  suffixes are legal in `offstubs`.
- `find_ints` dedups scanned instructions (`iseen`) — overlapping callee
  windows otherwise exhaust the 40K budget before reaching deep helpers
  like `resFileOpen`'s int21 path (which does `mov bx,ss; mov ds,bx`).
- `coverage.py` indexes cases globally across shard files — regens
  reshard cases without orphaning out.json results.

### Entry points probed (formerly skipped)

- `gfxInit` 5/5 AGREE, `openBlitClosePic` 5/5 AGREE
- `main` 5/5 AGREE-FAULT, `waitForKeyPress` 5/5 AGREE-FAULT (symmetric
  budget burn on poll loops)
- `runGameSession` incomplete — oracle reaches `device_io_or_halt` inside
  the session loop (real hardware access; sandbox limit, documented)

### Dedicated specs closed the partial cells

`dosunit/gen_partial.py` emits `dosunit/partial.json` — 12 cases / 36
vectors, all AGREE — resolving every probe-mix and both looping
incompletes:

- `allocBuffer` (END + START copies, ok + err arms): `call_stub`/
  `call_stub_c` force `dos_alloc` -> const segment symmetrically; the
  err arm additionally nops cleanup/print/exit on both sides so the
  post-exit fallthrough (return stored seg) is what gets compared.
- `drawStringCentered` START twin (alloc+zerofill): `dos_alloc` ->
  scratch DS; observes the zeroed window head.  EGAME twin (a
  different routine sharing the name): resident-driver lcall stubbed,
  ASCIIZ seeded at the string arg, rec fields + uppercased bytes obs.
- `drawClippedLineEx`/`drawClippedLineRegion`: every reachable call
  stubbed `zero` (symmetric with the cand thunk bodies); window-cell
  stores paired via the shared-DS demand map.
- `drawGaugeBar`: `fillRectBoth`'s driver lcalls stubbed (the real
  dispatcher writes into the runtime ljmp-slot table ->
  instruction_memory_write); record ptrs seeded at scratch cells so
  the callee's `[bx+4]` stores are observed; `[0x4efa]` toggles the
  gate per vector.
- `drawStoreIcons` lo/hi: oracle lcalls stubbed + dead-overlay
  drawString near-calls nopped; the es record ptr aimed at a seeded
  scratch window covering both `0x13` arms; first-lcall answer
  toggled for the `byte_98E6` gate.
- `loadPicFromFileAt`: `showPicFile` nopped (hand-asm PIC decoder
  loops on seeded bytes); `openFile`/`closeFile` run real code
  through int_stub + dsss_stub.

Infrastructure: `duspec.emit` gained `call_stub_c` (candidate-side
call stubbing, mirrors `call_stub`), `call_stub_exe` hashes sites at
4 bytes (EGAME multi-seg offsets exceed 0xffff), `dosunit16.py` keys
verdict sources by (group, id) so duplicate fn names across cases
(the two `drawStringCentered` twins) cannot cross-wire obs pairs,
and `gen_probe.py`'s driver is `__main__`-guarded so its BFS
collectors (`find_ints`, `pick_ds`, `call_patch`) are importable.

### Remaining known-partial cells

- incomplete: `sub_16076`/`sub_16486`/`sub_1714C`/`sub_17280`/
  `runGameSession` (in/out hardware io — unmodelable in the sandbox)
- artifact: 11 routines, all MATCH-verified byte-exact — diffs are
  binary-relative DS layouts, stub-callee asymmetry, or obs cross-wiring
  (see `dosunit/coverage.py` ARTIFACTS for per-routine reasons)

Final inventory: 83 dedicated + 212 probe-agree + 0 probe-mix +
11 artifact + 5 incomplete = 311 ported, **0 diff, 0 uncovered**.

# Notator Online 🎹

> The Atari ST Sequencer, in your browser

**🌐 Live Demo: [notator.online](https://notator.online)**

A browser-based player and parser for **Notator SL 3.21** `.SON` files, built with modern Web Audio and Web MIDI APIs. A tribute to the legendary C-Lab/eMagic Notator sequencer for the Atari ST.

## ✨ Features

- **Complete `.SON` parser** — all 14+ event types (confirmed via Ghidra decompilation of `NOTATOR.PRG`)
- **General MIDI playback** — realistic instrument sounds via [WebAudioFont](https://github.com/surikov/webaudiofont) (FluidR3 GM SoundFont)
- **Full GM drum kit** on channel 10 with real kick, snare, hi-hat, cymbal samples
- **Program Change** support — songs that specify instruments switch sounds correctly
- **Arrangement playback** — automatic pattern sequencing (auto-advance to next pattern)
- **Web MIDI output** — route audio to connected hardware synths/modules
- **Round-trip serializer** — parse → edit → write back byte-identical `.SON` files
- **SysEx chain support** — multi-record System Exclusive messages via continuation bit
- **Transport controls** — play, pause, stop, tempo adjustment
- **Track mute/solo** — per-track audio control
- **Demo files included** — 4 bundled `.SON` files from Notator tutorials

## 🛠 Tech Stack

| Layer     | Technology                                         |
| --------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| Framework | **Next.js 16** (App Router, static export)         |
| UI        | **React 19** + **Tailwind CSS 4**                  |
| Audio     | **WebAudioFont** (GM SoundFont) + **Web MIDI API** |
| Parser    | TypeScript — complete round-trip `.SON` format     |
| Hosting   | **Cloudflare Pages** (static)                      |

## 📁 Project Structure

```
notator-web/
├── app/                           # Next.js App Router
│   ├── layout.tsx                 # Root layout + metadata
│   ├── page.tsx                   # Landing page
│   ├── player/page.tsx            # Main player view
│   └── globals.css                # Notator dark theme
├── components/
│   ├── ui/FileDropZone.tsx        # Drag-and-drop .SON upload
│   ├── transport/TransportBar.tsx # Play/stop/pause/tempo controls
│   └── tracks/TrackList.tsx       # Track display + mute/solo
├── lib/
│   ├── son-parser/
│   │   ├── index.ts               # Full .SON parser (all event types)
│   │   ├── types.ts               # SonFile, TrackSlot, 14+ event types
│   │   └── serializer.ts          # Write .SON files back to binary
│   ├── midi/
│   │   ├── web-midi.ts            # Web MIDI API wrapper
│   │   └── synth-fallback.ts      # WebAudioFont GM synth engine
│   └── playback/
│       └── engine.ts              # Lookahead scheduler + pattern sequencing
├── public/
│   ├── demos/                     # Bundled .SON demo files
│   └── webaudiofont/              # Vendored WebAudioFont player
├── tools/
│   └── notator-floppy/               # Floppy disk reader tool
│       ├── notator_floppy.py          # CLI for disk detection/extraction
│       ├── notator_floppy_gui.py      # GUI for bulk transfers
│       ├── disk_reader.py             # Raw disk reading (macOS/Linux/Win)
│       └── atari_fat.py               # Atari ST FAT12 filesystem parser
├── types/
│   └── webaudiofont.d.ts          # TypeScript declarations
└── next.config.ts                 # Static export config
```

## 💾 Floppy Disk Companion Tool

A Python-based CLI and GUI for reading Atari ST floppy disks, extracting `.SON` files, and creating disk images. Perfect for bulk-transferring an entire collection of Notator floppies.

### Requirements

- Python 3.8+
- USB floppy drive
- `sudo` access on macOS/Linux for raw disk reading

### Quick Start

```bash
cd tools/notator-floppy

# CLI: Detect connected floppy drives
python3 notator_floppy.py detect

# CLI: Extract all files from a floppy
sudo python3 notator_floppy.py extract --output-dir ./my_songs

# CLI: Create a raw disk image backup (.ST format)
sudo python3 notator_floppy.py image my_backup.st

# GUI: Launch the bulk transfer interface
python3 notator_floppy_gui.py
```

### Bulk Transfer Workflow

The GUI automates the process of archiving a large floppy collection:

1. **Insert** an Atari ST floppy disk
2. The tool **reads** the disk, **extracts** all files, and **saves** a raw `.ST` disk image
3. A completion sound plays and the disk is **auto-ejected**
4. **Insert** the next disk — the tool auto-detects it and repeats

All extracted files and disk images are saved to `tools/notator-floppy/floppy_archive/` (gitignored).

## 🚀 Getting Started

```bash
# Install dependencies
npm install

# Start dev server
npm run dev

# Build for production (static export)
npm run build

# Preview the static build
npx serve out
```

Open [http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000) to see the app, or visit the live version at [notator.online](https://notator.online).

## 🎹 Usage

1. Open the player at [notator.online/player](https://notator.online/player) (or `/player` locally)
2. Drag & drop a `.SON` file or click one of the demo files
3. Press **Start** — audio plays through:
   - **WebAudioFont GM synth** — realistic instrument sounds (default)
   - **Connected MIDI devices** — via Web MIDI API (if available)
4. Songs automatically advance through patterns in the arrangement
5. Use **Mute (M)** and **Solo (S)** buttons on individual tracks
6. Adjust tempo with the tempo input field

## 📄 .SON File Format

The `.SON` format is a proprietary binary format used by Notator SL/Creator on the Atari ST. This parser supports the complete format, verified against Ghidra decompilation of `NOTATOR.PRG 3.21`:

### File Layout

| Region         | Offset   | Description                                       |
| -------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Header         | `0x0000` | Magic, tempo, ticks/measure, instrument names     |
| Channel Config | `0x0330` | MIDI channels, programs, volumes, pans (16 slots) |
| Arrangement    | `0x0370` | Pattern sequencing data                           |
| Track Data     | `0x5AC8` | Boundary-separated track slots                    |

### Event Types (6 bytes each)

| Status (& 0xF0) | Type             | Description                             |
| --------------- | ---------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `0x00`          | Meta             | Pattern end markers, system events      |
| `0x30`          | Bar Marker       | Bar/pattern boundary markers            |
| `0x40`          | Track Setup      | Track initialization data               |
| `0x60`          | Track Config     | Filter flags, channel/port assignment   |
| `0x70`          | Notation         | Display-only notation data              |
| `0x80`          | Note Off         | MIDI note release                       |
| `0x90`          | Note On          | MIDI note with velocity                 |
| `0xA0`          | Aftertouch       | Polyphonic key pressure                 |
| `0xB0`          | Control Change   | CC messages (sustain, modulation, etc.) |
| `0xC0`          | Program Change   | GM instrument selection                 |
| `0xD0`          | Channel Pressure | Monophonic aftertouch                   |
| `0xE0`          | Pitch Wheel      | Pitch bend data                         |
| `0xF0`          | SysEx            | System Exclusive (multi-record chains)  |

### Key Details

- **768 ticks per measure** (192 ticks per beat in 4/4)
- **Track boundaries**: `7F FF FF FF` (type A) or `00 0F FF FF` (type B)
- **SysEx continuation**: `byte[5] & 0x80` chains records into single messages
- **Track preamble**: 24-byte header + 8-byte name + 14-byte config = 46 bytes per slot

## 🔧 Round-Trip Serialization

The parser preserves all raw data for byte-exact reconstruction:

```typescript
import { parseSonFile } from "./lib/son-parser";
import { serializeSonFile } from "./lib/son-parser/serializer";

const buffer = await file.arrayBuffer();
const sonFile = parseSonFile(buffer);

// Modify sonFile.header, events, etc.

const output = serializeSonFile(sonFile);
// output is byte-identical to input if no edits were made
```

## 🔬 Reverse Engineering

The `.SON` format specification was derived from:

1. **Hex analysis** of 15 `.SON` files from Notator tutorials
2. **Ghidra decompilation** of `NOTATOR.PRG 3.21` using a custom [RetroGhidra](https://github.com/hippietrail/RetroGhidra) Atari ST loader (ported to Ghidra 12 API)
3. **`FUN_000149dc`** — the 666-line main event dispatcher (`switch(status & 0xF0)`)
4. Prior work by [Simon Cozens (son2midi)](https://github.com/simoncozens/son2midi)

## 📝 License

MIT

## 🙏 Credits

- **Notator SL** — C-Lab / eMagic (Gerhard Lengeling)
- **son2midi** — [Simon Cozens](https://github.com/simoncozens/son2midi) for initial .SON reverse engineering
- **WebAudioFont** — [Sergey Surikov](https://github.com/surikov/webaudiofont) for GM SoundFont samples
- **RetroGhidra** — [Andrew Dunstan](https://github.com/hippietrail/RetroGhidra) for the Atari ST Ghidra loader
- **Atari ST** community for preserving these files

sammiq-st25-readme-md.text:
# Star Trek: 25th Anniversary (CD, DOS) decompilation

Matching decompilation of `STARTREK.EXE`, the DOS executable from the CD release. The aim is C source that compiles to the original machine code with the original compiler. Progress is measured, and functions are compared, with [objdiff](https://github.com/encounter/objdiff).

The away-mission rooms' scripts are machine code too, but they live in the game's data files rather than the EXE. They are decompiled to assembly source separately: see [Room scripts](#room-scripts-rdf).

## The original build

| | |
|---|---|
| Compiler | Microsoft C 6.00A (`tools/C600`) |
| Memory model | Medium (`/AM`): far code, near data. Each `.C` file has its own `NAME_TEXT` segment |
| Game code flags | `/AM /G2 /qc /Gs`: 286 instructions, quick compile, no stack checks |
| Runtime | `MLIBCR` + `MLIBFP` + `EM` (8087 emulator), plus `LIBH` helpers |

These flags are what the first matched functions need. Quick-compile (`/qc`) code is easy to spot: every function starts `enter n,0 / push si / push di`, and conditionals compile to `jcc short` over `jmp near`.

## Setup

You need Python 3.11+, ninja, [emu2](https://github.com/dmsc/emu2) on `PATH`, and a Rust toolchain (to build objdiff and exepack).

```sh
python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
tools/objdiff/build.sh             # patched objdiff + objdiff-cli -> tools/bin
tools/exepack/build.sh             # exepack -> tools/bin
.venv/bin/python configure.py      # writes build.ninja and objdiff.json
ninja                              # split targets, build everything
ninja progress                     # progress summary
```

These inputs are not in git, so supply your own copies:
- `orig/CD/TREKCD/STARTREK.EXE` (the original EXE, as shipped; `configure.py` checks it against `config/orig.sha1`, or run `sha1sum -c config/orig.sha1`)
- `tools/C600/` (the Microsoft C 6.00A installation: `BIN`, `INCLUDE`, `LIB`)
- `tools/MASM50/` (the Microsoft Assembler 5.0 installation: `BIN`, `INC`)

The original was linked with `/EXEPACK`, so it is compressed. The build unpacks it with David Fifield's [exepack](https://www.bamsoftware.com/software/exepack/) (`exepack -d`) into `build/exe/STARTREK.EXE`, which is the image every tool reads, and IDA too. Set `$EXEPACK` to use an exepack other than `tools/bin/exepack` or the one on `PATH`.

Open `objdiff.json` in `tools/bin/objdiff` (the GUI) for the interactive diff. It rebuilds base objects as you save.

### Rebuilding the EXE

`STARTREK.MAK` is an NMAKE makefile that rebuilds the whole program with the original tools. It compiles the C units with CL, assembles the assembly modules with MASM, combines the runtime into `MLIBCE.LIB` the way C 6.00 SETUP does, and links with LINK 5.10. `tools/dosbuild.py` runs it in DOSBox (dosbox-staging, headless) and compares the result with the shipped EXE:

```sh
.venv/bin/python tools/dosbuild.py      # -> build/dos/STARTREK.EXE, .MAP, NMAKE.LOG
.venv/bin/python tools/dosbuild.py /A   # rebuild everything
```

emu2 can't run this build: NMAKE needs a command processor, and LINK 5.10 goes wrong under emu2 with this many objects.

The original was linked with `/EXEPACK`, and so is the rebuild. The two packed files are compared directly, then both are unpacked with exepack and compared again, where each difference stays at the address it affects.

The link options are `/NOI /NOD /NONULLSDOSSEG /EXEPACK /ST:0xF00`. Without `/NONULLSDOSSEG`, LINK puts 16 zero bytes at the start of `_TEXT`. Modules link in segment order, seg000 to seg036. `asm/t35052` opens `_TEXT` (`.CODE _TEXT`), and the C runtime follows it. `asm/t3715C`, `asm/t3A200` and `asm/t41E20` aren't linked, because they are library code that LINK pulls in itself. seg006 is compiled with `/Zi`: its reference to `__aDBused` is what brings in the runtime's `dbscrswp`.

`src/BSS.ASM`, generated by `tools/genbss.py` from `symbols.txt`, comes last. LINK lays communals (uninitialized globals) out in an order of its own that depends on the original, lost variable names. So BSS.ASM defines each one as a public at its original address, in `c_common` and `FAR_BSS`, sized to the next symbol so that unreferenced variables keep their space. The C files' tentative definitions resolve to these publics. The publics must carry DGROUP (`ASSUME DS:DGROUP`), because the C objects' references take their frame from the public. BSS.ASM also declares the runtime's `XOB`/`XO`/`XOE` and `EMULATOR_DATA`, which keeps the segment order. It's a reproduction aid, not recovered source; regenerate it after renaming or resizing a `.bss` symbol.

#### Status: done

The rebuilt program image (all code and data) is identical to the original, and so are both EXE headers. The rebuilt EXE runs and plays in DOSBox. Two discrepancies remain, and the project accepts both as they are:

- **Relocation order.** The relocation table has the same 4,797 entries as the original, but 26 of them are in a different order. LINK writes them in the order it processes modules, so the original fed it some modules in a different order (one example: a relocation in seg028 comes before t35052's). DOS applies every relocation when it loads the program, whatever their order, so the program in memory is the same byte for byte.
- **`.bss` layout from `BSS.ASM`.** The uninitialized globals sit at their original addresses only because `BSS.ASM` pins them there. The original's layout came from LINK's own placement of the communals, which depends on variable names that are lost. The data starts out zeroed either way, so the program doesn't depend on how the layout was produced.

Neither affects how the game runs.

## Layout

```
config/ida_export.txt   IDA database export (tools/ida/export.idc)
config/symbols.txt      every function/data symbol: address, kind, size, name
config/units.txt        units (translation units) and their address ranges
src/<unit>.c            decompiled source, one file per unit
src/rdf/<room>.asm      room scripts, one file per .RDF (config/rdf.txt lists them)
include/                shared headers
tools/                  build tooling (below)
build/target/           target objects split from the EXE (generated)
build/base/             objects compiled from src/ or taken from the C library
```

Addresses are IDA linear addresses, so `seg000:0018` is `10018`. The load module sits at paragraph `0x1000`.

### Units

Units are generated by `tools/init_config.py`:

- **`segNNN`**: one per game code segment, which is one per original `.C` file. Rename a unit once you know its original file name. Names must be DOS 8.3 compatible, because the compiler runs under DOS.
- **`lib/<module>`**: C runtime modules found in the EXE. Their base objects come straight from the library, so they count as complete.
- **`asm/tXXXXX`**: parts of `_TEXT` that aren't library code (probably game assembly modules).
- **`far/segNNN`, `data/dXXXXX`, `data/stack`**: far data segments, and the parts of DGROUP not yet assigned to a unit.

### Symbols

`config/symbols.txt` holds linker names, so C functions and variables carry a leading underscore. IDA's placeholder names become `_sub_10018`, `_word_4B464` and so on, which lets C code use `sub_10018` as is. Rename a symbol by editing its line here (or in IDA, then re-export and re-run `tools/init_config.py`, which keeps your existing non-placeholder names). Names and addresses must be unique: the tools look symbols up both ways, so loading `symbols.txt` stops with an error that lists any repeats. Two functions that IDA named alike need distinct names (`LoadMenu` in seg014, `LoadGameMenu` in seg019).

## Decompilation notes

How to decompile and match functions, the code patterns of the original compiler, data placement, the room-script format and the tooling are all in [docs/decompilation.md](docs/decompilation.md).

## Room scripts (.RDF)

Each away-mission room has a `.RDF` file in `DATA.001` (53 rooms: `DEMON0`–`VENG8`). Besides the room's header (`Rdf` in `include/room.h`: depth scaling, exits, entry positions), polygons and strings, it holds the room's scripts, which are 16-bit x86 code. `LoadRoom` loads the file whole and `CallScript` calls into it with `SI` = `&room` (the `RoomState`), and the scripts call back through the far pointer at offset 0 (`ScriptService` in `src/seg008.c`). The scripts were written in assembly, not C: strings sit inline with `jmp` over them, arguments are pushed in two different styles, the helpers take arguments in registers, and some bodies run into the next script's header.

The rooms' scripts are disassembled too: each room is MASM 5.0 source in `src/rdf/<room>.asm` that assembles to the original file byte for byte (`ninja rdf`), with every script, variable and object named and commented. [docs/decompilation.md](docs/decompilation.md#room-scripts-rdf) describes the file format, the script interface and the tooling (`tools/rdf.py`).

### Quirks of the original

The scripts are hand-written and contain some oddities and outright bugs. Each source lists its own at the top. Across the rooms:

- In most rooms the last script's `next` is the helpers' code, which the engine then reads as one more script. Its "key" and "next" are instruction bytes, and the bogus `next` is past `scripts_end`, so the search stops. VENG2 is larger than that bogus `next`, so its search carries on through the middle of its code and reads two more fake scripts. One of them has the key `FF 1E 00 00`, which `RunWildScripts` matches against any message about object 1Eh.
- FEATHER3, FEATHER5 and VENG3 have scripts that run on into the next script's header, or jump to it, and execute its six bytes as code.
- DEMON1 pushes the three arguments that four `Anim` calls share before choosing between them; the fourth case pops them (`pop ax` three times) and pushes its own. One script there pushes a call's arguments and drops them again, a call that was taken out.
- The TRIAL rooms, SINS3 and VENG2 build some conversations at run time in `talk_buf` and go on through a jump table (`choice_jumps`) that the script fills in with the code for each choice.
- TRIAL2 skips a block with a `jmp`, and SINS1 has code after a `retf`. Both are dead code (`code=` in `config/rdf.txt`).
- DEMON4's conversation with the Nauian tests a flag that nothing sets, so its own "join the Federation" ending is never reached; the same lines play when the Nauian turns the key.
- In LOVE0, the script for getting door 8 has no body: its entry is the next script's header, whose six bytes run as code before its `jmp`. The doors' own answer is left unreachable behind it.
- The LOVE rooms' communicator scripts have four cases, all playing the same placeholder lines recorded for other missions. LOVE3 tests a flag nothing sets (so the insulation can always be taken). LOVE4 awards the water's point every time, because it sets the flag to 2 but tests it against 1. In LOVE5, two scripts share the key for phasers on Preax, so the second never runs.
- Two MUDD scripts have mangled keys that can never match. MUDD2's McCoy-tricorder-on-Mudd script is keyed `45h, 8, 0, 0` instead of `MSG_USE, IT_MTRICOR, 8, 0`. MUDD3's use-the-screen script has its two objects swapped. Also in MUDD2, using a bed once McCoy is ready walks Kirk with a message nothing handles. In MUDD5, firing the alien device marks it used without the +5 that every other MUDD room gives.
- FEATHER6 has two scripts keyed `MSG_USE, IT_ROCK, ANY`, so the second never runs. FEATHER5 gives Kirk McCoy's line "Jim! Are you out of your mind?".
- SINS0, SINS1 and SINS4 each have a second script with the same key as an earlier one (talking to Mosher, talking to Spock, Spock on the lock), which never runs. SINS3 has a script keyed on using object 20h, which is no item. SINS5 tests five point-once flags it never sets, so those points come every time.
- Both of VENG2's conversation menus end in a debug line from a speaker "wes" ("kirk dialog error.", "power allocation error.") for a choice that can't happen. VENG8's script for Kije reaching the transporter pad also answers a walk that is never started, and counts arrivals as if two crewmen were walking there.

## Amiga version

The AGA (A1200) release can be put into `orig/AMIGA` for analysis. The decompilation doesn't use it, and nothing below is part of the build.

Graphics: the same as the DOS floppy

- All 5,700 bitmaps it shares with the floppy have identical pixels. They're all 320×200, 256-colour images, with only the 8-byte header byte-swapped.
AGA can show 256 colours, so nothing was reduced.
- The palettes are the same colours. DOS stores 6-bit values (0–63) and the Amiga stores them scaled up to 8-bit, so there's no finer colour detail.
- Every other shared graphics and room file (ANM, SHP, R3S, XOR, MAP, IW, PRI) is the same size as on floppy. They are straight byte-swapped conversions.
- 1,293 extra .BAM files. Each one works out at exactly 9 bits per pixel: 8 bitplanes plus a mask, the format the Amiga's blitter draws. They hold the
room background animations (bridge lights, flickers and so on) as finished frames. On DOS, a .BAN file is a stream of pixel changes drawn into the
background. On the Amiga, the .BAN is just a list of which BAM frames to show (e.g. S5R5L1.BAN is 52 bytes vs 1.1K on DOS). The animations are the
same, only stored differently.
- The CD's redrawn title logo isn't here: GOLDLOGO matches the floppy.

Music: a separate implementation

- DOS: Music is MIDI sequences played through the Miles AIL driver on AdLib, MT-32, PC speaker or Tandy (.AD/.MT/.PC/.TD).
- Amiga: The Amiga version doesn't use the DOS XMIDI music. Its `TREK*.SNG` files are "The Player 4.1A" (`P41A`) tracker modules with the samples taken out. The letter before `.SNG` names the bank they draw on (`SAMPLES.A`–`D`), and `snd.bin` is the 68k replayer. `tools/amiga_music.py OUT` turns them into ProTracker `.mod` files, plus `.wav` files with `--wav` (needs an ffmpeg built with libopenmpt). The script's docstring describes the format and how the player's effects differ from ProTracker's. Again, it's a standalone tool: nothing in the build calls it.

RDF room scripts: still x86

The Amiga RDFs contain the same x86 machine code as DOS, and the Amiga executable has an 8086 interpreter built in. [src/rdf/i8086.c](src/rdf/i8086.c) is a hand decompilation of that interpreter, kept for reference only. It isn't compiled.

Content: floppy-based, with some text fixes

- Some text edits that later appear on the CD, Overall there are about 700 changed lines in the room scripts compared with the floppy.
- Extra files it has that neither DOS version has: room graphics for TRIAL9 and TUG9 (BMP/PRI/MAP/IW), STARS00–15, and CREDIT06. The Amiga has the TRIAL9 background but no TRIAL9.RDF, while the CD has the RDF but no background. So a room 9 seems to have been designed and then abandoned, with each port shipping a different part of it.

sammiq-stjr-readme-md.text:
# Star Trek: Judgment Rites (CD, DOS) decompilation

A matching decompilation of `TREKJR.EXE`, the DOS executable of the Judgment Rites CD release (dated 7 Oct 1995). The goal is C source that the original compiler turns back into the original machine code. Progress is measured function by function with [objdiff](https://github.com/encounter/objdiff). The whole program can also be relinked with the original linker and compared with the shipped EXE.

## Status

| Category | Code | Functions | Data |
|---|---|---|---|
| Game code | 126,381 / 144,425 bytes (87.5%) | 825 / 854 | 31,940 / 31,940 (100%) |
| C runtime | 22,971 / 22,971 (100%) | 368 / 368 | 2,444 / 2,444 (100%) |
| Uninitialized (communals, stack) | | | reproduced by `src/BSS.ASM` |

The fuzzy match over all code is 99.68%. Every function is decompiled, and every function that doesn't match yet is within a few instructions of the original (see [Differences from the original](#differences-from-the-original)).

"Code" counts the bytes of functions that match exactly. The 86 bytes of "Game data" are runtime data between library modules (`data/d3F225`, `data/d3F290`, `data/d3F4D9`) that no module has been found for; the link places them correctly anyway.

## The original build

| | |
|---|---|
| Compiler | Microsoft C/C++ 7.00 (`tools/C700`), runtime "Copyright (c) 1992" |
| Memory model | Medium (`/AM`): far code, near data |
| Game code flags | `/AM /G2 /Ox /FPa /Zp1`, the same for every file |
| Assembler | MASM 5.0 (`mvelib`, `seg027`, `seg028`, `asm/t2D688`) |
| Runtime | `MLIBCA.LIB` (medium model, alternate math) and `OLDNAMES.LIB`. C 7.00's setup only builds `MLIBCA.LIB` when alternate math is chosen |
| Link | `/NOI /NOD /EXEPACK /PACKCODE /FARCALLTRANSLATION /STACK:0x12E8` |

The flags were confirmed by testing alternatives on files that already match:
- `/Ox` is right. Turning off any of its `/O` letters breaks functions that match today, or changes nothing.
- C 6.00 matches far fewer functions.
- The older C 7.00 (prior to any post-release patches) has identical compiler passes.
- `/FPa` makes floating point call the runtime's `__aF*` helpers, as the original does. Its code is the same as `/FPc`'s; what tells them apart is the library.

What the tooling has to deal with:

- **Packed code.** LINK `/PACKCODE` merged every file's code segment into three segments (0000h, 0BD6h and 1B98h, whose tail is the C runtime's `_TEXT`). Nothing in the EXE marks where one file ends. Units were carved out by hand, from the order of functions and the data each file uses.
- **Far call translation.** LINK turned far calls inside a packed segment into `nop; push cs; call near` (`90 0E E8`). `project.load_exe()` turns them back into `call far` with a segment fixup, so every tool sees an image that compares with compiled objects. A 4-byte `push cs; call near` without the `nop` is the compiler's own call to a function in the same file.
- **No IDA database.** `tools/analyze.py` disassembles the EXE by recursive descent from every far call, near call and far code pointer. It writes `build/analysis.txt` in the format of an IDA export, so an export from `tools/ida/export.idc` can replace it.
- **DGROUP** is 2B87h (linear 3B870h). The far data segments are 290Eh, 2B0Eh and 2B3Eh. String literals are in the game's `_DATA`, not `CONST`.

## Setup

You need Python 3.11+, ninja, **dosemu2** and a Rust toolchain (for objdiff and exepack).

```sh
python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
tools/objdiff/build.sh             # patched objdiff + objdiff-cli -> tools/bin
tools/exepack/build.sh             # exepack -> tools/bin
.venv/bin/python configure.py      # writes build.ninja and objdiff.json
ninja                              # unpack, analyse, split targets, build base objects
ninja progress                     # progress summary (tools/progress.py build/report.json -v per unit)
```

These inputs are not in git, so supply your own copies:
- `orig/CD/`: the CD's files. `orig/CD/TREKJR.EXE` must match `config/orig.sha1`.
- `tools/C700/`: Microsoft C/C++ 7.00 (`BIN`, `INCLUDE`, `LIB`), with the alternate math libraries installed (`LIB/MLIBCA.LIB`).
- `tools/MASM50/`: Microsoft Assembler 5.0, for the assembly units.

### Running the compiler

C 7.00's compiler passes are 32-bit DOS-extended programs (DOSX32 + `MS32KRNL.DLL`, a cut-down Win32 kernel) that need a DPMI host. Microsoft supported only a Windows 3.x DOS box or Qualitas 386-MAX. emu2 has no DPMI. In DOSBox, both HDPMI32 and CWSDPMI start it, but MS32KRNL then faults during its own start-up.

**dosemu2** works. `tools/cc.py` runs each compile in it (`dosemu -dumb -K <project> -E <batch>`) with the project root as the current drive, so paths must be 8.3 and inside the project. A compile takes about 0.7 s, and each one gets its own `TMP` directory so ninja can run them in parallel.

dosemu2's default shell, comcom64, needs the dj64 runtime, which Fedora's packages don't install. So `cc.py` sets `DOSEMU2_COMCOM_DIR=/usr/share/comcom32`; override it with that variable. `$DOSEMU` selects the dosemu binary.

## Layout

```
config/symbols.txt   every function/data symbol: address, kind, size, name
config/units.txt     units (translation units) and their address ranges
config/relocs.txt    explicit references the analysis can't tell from numbers
config/aliases.txt   library names sharing an address (generated)
src/<unit>.c         decompiled source, one file per unit (.asm for assembly)
src/BSS.ASM          communal layout for the relink (generated, tools/genbss.py)
include/             shared headers
TREKJR.MAK           NMAKE makefile for a full rebuild under DOS
build/analysis.txt   generated disassembly structure (tools/analyze.py)
build/target/        target objects split from the EXE (generated)
build/base/          objects compiled from src/ or taken from the C library
build/dos/           the relinked TREKJR.EXE (tools/dosbuild.py)
```

Addresses are linear, with the load module at paragraph 1000h: `seg001:6056` is `1BD60 + 6056 = 21DB6`.

### Units

- **`segNNN`, `space`, `demo`, `acmp`, `cfg`, `iff`**: the game's C files, one run of code each, in the original's link order. Unit names must be 8.3, because the compiler runs under DOS.
- **`mvelib`, `seg027`, `seg028`, `asm/t2D688`**: assembly modules (the movie player library, and hand-written routines such as `PlayDelta`).
- **`lib/<module>`**: C runtime modules (`tools/libmatch.py`), built straight from `MLIBCA.LIB` or `MLIBCE.LIB` (the two share the non-floating-point modules). Their target relocations come from the library's own fixups. When a library has two modules of one name (the near and far `chkstk.asm`), `lib=LIB:name@N` picks one. Data-only modules (`_file.c`, `ctype.asm`, `cmiscdat.asm`, `huge.asm`) are units of their own, placed by hand.
- **`far/segNNN`, `data/dXXXXX`, `data/stack`**: far data and DGROUP pieces that belong to no file: the communals, the stack, and the few runtime bytes above.

Each file's statics are declared `static` in their source, in the original's address order, so its `_BSS` matches per unit. C 7.00 also puts its buffers for functions that return structs there.

## Workflow

1. Name things: `tools/rename.py _sub_21DB6 _ListInit` updates symbols.txt, relocs.txt and the sources.
2. Edit `src/<unit>.c`, then run `ninja progress`, or open `objdiff.json` in `tools/bin/objdiff`.
3. Use `tools/fdiff.py UNIT SYMBOL` for a side-by-side view, and `tools/disasm.py ADDR [END]` for the original.
   `tools/relcheck.py [UNIT...]` lists functions whose instructions reference different symbols from the original's. objdiff can score these 100%: a call to the wrong one of two near-identical functions, statics laid out in the wrong order, stores to two fields in the opposite order.
4. `tools/splitunit.py START END name` carves a new unit out of an address range.
5. After changing how the EXE is analysed, `tools/init_config.py` regenerates symbols.txt (keeping every name you've given) and adds newly found library modules to units.txt. `--force` rebuilds units.txt from scratch and loses your splits.

Notes on getting C 7.00 to produce a given instruction sequence (loop forms, copy variables, register choice) are kept with the sources' comments and in commit messages.

## Full rebuild

`tools/dosbuild.py` links `build/dos/TREKJR.EXE` from the objects ninja builds (`build/obj/`). It runs C 7.00's LINK under dosemu2 with the original's options and libraries, in the units' code order. It then compares the result with `TREKJR.EXE`, both packed and unpacked. Run ninja first.

`TREKJR.MAK` does the whole build the old way, with NMAKE under DOS: compile, assemble, link. Its result is the same EXE. Before running it, `SET PATH=\TOOLS\C700\BIN` and `SET INCLUDE=\TOOLS\C700\INCLUDE`.

- **`_BSS`**: each file's statics come out in link order, as in the original.
- **`c_common`** and the far communals (`FAR_BSS`): LINK lays these out in an order of its own that depends on the lost variable names. `src/BSS.ASM` is generated by `tools/genbss.py` from `symbols.txt` and linked last. It defines each communal at its original address. It's a reproduction aid, not recovered source; regenerate it after renaming or resizing a symbol there.
- **Layout**: every segment comes out in the original's order and alignment (code, far data, DGROUP, BSS, stack), with the original stack size. The only cause of differences left is the code of the functions that don't match yet.

## Differences from the original

The relinked EXE is 64 bytes shorter than the original, both packed (184,826 vs 184,890) and unpacked (202,448 vs 202,512). The header's `SS` and `CS` are 4 paragraphs lower, and `minalloc` 1. All of this comes from 15 functions whose compiled size differs from the original's. Each one moves every address after it, so far more bytes differ than the functions themselves account for: far calls and data references all change. Only 15.5% of the packed file, or 24.0% unpacked, is equal byte for byte. Once those 15 sizes are right, the rest of the image should line up.

### Functions of the wrong size

| Unit | Function | Size difference (bytes) | What differs |
|---|---|---|---|
| seg008 | `InputBox` | −22 | a local stored as a word in the original stays in a register; key cases branch differently |
| seg008 | `ScriptService` | +12 | a pointer kept in `si` in the original is reloaded from the stack; branch layout in the switch |
| space | `Evaluate` | −8 | `pct` lives on the stack in the original, so its dead store `pct = 1` survives; register choice in the clamp |
| seg008 | `Converse` | −6 | the original points `DS` at a far record; ours uses `ES:` overrides and one more local |
| seg014 | `MenuLoop` | −4 | a 32-bit sum evaluated in a different order (as in `MenuWait`) |
| demo | `PlayDpAnim` | −4 | ours has a 2-byte larger frame, so every local's slot moves |
| cfg | `CfgOpen` | −4 | a dead store (`mov [bp-2],dx`) the original keeps |
| seg015 | `StreamInit` | +4 | a far pointer argument (`&s->field`) built differently |
| demo | `PlayMovie` | +4 | the original loads `heap0` with `les bx` instead of keeping it in `si` |
| seg003 | `FindFile` | −2 | a field store and an index multiply (×7 by shifts) in a different order |
| seg005 | `ReadPointer` | −2 | the original multiplies in `cx`, then reloads `mouse_x` from memory; ours multiplies in `si` |
| seg008 | `EnterRoom` | −2 | a comparison done in a register instead of on the stack |
| seg008 | `CrewSay` | −2 | a local in `di` vs on the stack, and slot order |
| seg015 | `PlayMusicSeq` | −2 | an extra `mov ax,cx` before the push |
| acmp | `AcmpOpen` | −1 | `di` vs `si`, and the original has one more local |

By file, the code segments differ by:

| Segment | Original | Rebuilt | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| SEG003 | 105Eh | 105Ch | −2 |
| SEG005 | 994h | 992h | −2 |
| SEG008 | 4FE0h | 4FCCh | −20 |
| SEG014 | 13A0h | 139Ch | −4 |
| SEG015 | 25CCh | 25CEh | +2 |
| DEMO | CD9h | CDAh | +1 (alignment) |
| SPACE | 1BA8h | 1BA0h | −8 |
| CFG | 386h | 382h | −4 |

ACMP's −1 disappears in word alignment.

### Right size, different code

These 14 functions don't change any address. They differ only inside themselves:

| Unit | Function | Match | What differs |
|---|---|---|---|
| seg009 | `PickItem` | 99.99% | one register (`si,dx` vs `si,di`) |
| seg014 | `MenuMove` | 99.98% | stack-slot order of locals |
| seg015 | `SoundInit` | 99.97% | register choice |
| seg012 | `Turbolift` | 99.97% | stack-slot order |
| seg008 | `CheckRegions` | 99.97% | one register |
| seg007 | `BuildRemap` | 99.95% | stack-slot order |
| seg001 | `Intercept` | 99.91% | stack-slot order |
| seg000 | `StartTalk` | 99.91% | stack-slot order |
| seg023 | `DrawStars` | 99.85% | a far pointer copied through a second local |
| seg008 | `PickObject` | 99.01% | call and argument order |
| acmp | `AcmpRead` | 98.87% | comparison operand order (`cmp ax,[x]; jbe` vs `cmp [x],ax; jae`) |
| seg014 | `MenuWait` | 97.12% | a 32-bit sum evaluated in a different order (`ticks` loaded first); operand order, casts, `volatile` and split assignments don't change it |
| space | `EncounterTick` | 95.11% | shared vs duplicated return epilogues |
| seg015 | `PlayDigi` | 92.41% | the original has a 2-byte frame (`enter 2,0`), ours has none |

### Hidden differences

`tools/relcheck.py` finds one function that objdiff scores 100% but whose code isn't the original's: `AcmpUnary` (acmp) loads `rbyte` and `rlast` in the opposite order for `(cur.rbyte ^ cur.rlast) & 1`. Neither operand order, casts nor field types change C 7.00's choice.

Two kinds of mistake it caught are worth checking for when a file is done:
- **Static layout.** C 7.00 lays out a file's statics in the order they were *first declared*, and an `extern` in a header counts. `include/menu.h` declared `menu_sel` before `menu_count`, which swapped the two in seg014's `_BSS`.
- **Library modules with the same code.** `ctran.asm` (pow, log, log10, exp) and `csqrt.asm` + `ctrig.asm` (sqrt, sin, cos, tan) differ only in fixed-up bytes. `tools/libmatch.py` now also checks a module's `_DATA` (here the function names) against the EXE.

### What's been tried

- **Other compilers and flags:** see [The original build](#the-original-build). Nothing beats C 7.00 `/Ox`, and no single flag fixes these functions.
- **Source constructs:** these do change register and slot choices, and fixed several functions. Examples: index loops vs pointer loops, a copy variable, `return -2` vs `return n`, merged conditions, block-local declarations, and `unsigned` vs `int`. Pulling an assignment out of an expression into its own statement (`x = e; f(x)` vs `f(x = e)`) fixed `CanWalk` and `BridgeKey`. A search that tried every such hoist, the reverse fold, swapping adjacent independent assignments and splitting chained ones in all the remaining functions found nothing more: the variants that fix a size do it by making the function less like the original.

Most of the remaining differences look like C 7.00's register allocator making a different choice for an expression the source doesn't pin down. The dead stores in `Evaluate` and `CfgOpen` are part of this: they survive in the original because the variable lives on the stack there, not in a register.

agershun-hexic-readme-md.text:
# HEXIS - Hexagonal Tetris

A recreation of the classic DOS game HEXIS (circa 1987-1988).

## Play Online

**[Play HEXIS in your browser!](https://agershun.github.io/hexic/)**

The online version runs the original DOS executable via js-dos emulator.

## About

HEXIS is a Tetris-like puzzle game with hexagonal cells instead of squares. The original game was written in Borland Pascal with BGI graphics for DOS.

This project includes:
- **Original DOS game** running in browser via js-dos
- **Python recreation** using pygame
- **Reverse engineering documentation**

## Controls

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| 7 / Left / Numpad 7 | Move Left |
| 9 / Right / Numpad 9 | Move Right |
| 8 / Up / Numpad 8 | Rotate |
| 4 / Space / Numpad 4 | Drop |
| 1 / Numpad 1 | Toggle Next Preview |
| 3 / Numpad 3 | Toggle Sound |
| 6 / Numpad 6 | Increase Level |
| Esc | Restart |
| F10 | Boss Key |

## Running Locally

### Browser Version (Original DOS)
```bash
python3 -m http.server 8080
# Open http://localhost:8080
```

### Python Version
```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install pygame
python src/hexis.py
```

## Project Structure

```
hexic/
├── index.html              # Web page with js-dos emulator
├── data/
│   ├── HEXIS.EXE          # Original DOS executable
│   └── hexis.jsdos        # js-dos bundle
├── src/
│   ├── hexis.py           # Python recreation
│   └── HEXIS.PAS          # Reconstructed Pascal source
└── docs/
    └── HEXIS_REVERSE_ENGINEERING.md
```

## Technical Details

- **Original**: Borland Pascal, BGI graphics, EGA 640x350
- **Python version**: pygame, 2x scaled display
- **Web version**: js-dos (DOSBox in browser)

## License

This is a fan recreation for educational purposes.

smu1zel-wintext-re-readme-md.text:
# Palantir WinText Reversing and Decoding

## What is this?

This is a set of Python scripts written by Google’s Gemini 3.1 model as a research project to study the Palantir WinText .WT (word processing) and .MTF (images) file formats from the late 1980s. Everything here is reverse-engineered with no documentation used (it doesn’t exist).

## How?

As said before, Gemini wrote all the code here, except for this README and my sample files. The WTTOWRI (WinText to Windows Write) converter included with the program was very helpful as a free parser to reference, and, going off the 8086 assembly, Gemini and I were able to figure out how the format works more efficiently. It also helps that the converter was only around a few tens of functions, which is small compared to the main WinText executable, which is both a Windows program (IDA doesn’t do as well with NE compared to DOS) and significantly larger.

## Why?

I saw [some on social media](https://x.com/ammaar/status/2030392563534893381) using OpenAI’s Codex to reverse engineer old DOS software and reimplement them, so I was inspired to try to do the same with an early Windows program, just with Gemini instead of Codex.

I also wanted to revive a long-forgotten word processor format.

## Alright, so what can I do with this?

wt_parser takes .WT files and turns them into HTML data. It doesn’t support images, but it can work for basic documents.

wt_writer can synthetically create WinText documents without, well, WinText. The files do open in WinText, though you currently don’t have many styles and options. This was basically a test to see how well we could replicate the format.

mtf_parser accepts proprietary .MTF image files and converts them into PNGs.

wt_to_docx is an interesting one. We use the python-docx library and a lot of parsing logic to convert .WT files into .DOCX files, which a modern word processor can read. Images are handled as well with mtf_parser. Most things are faithfully reconstructed, though fonts should be considered best-effort.

FORMAT_SPEC.md is basically a reference cheat sheet of the format, generated with 3 Flash. You’ll probably find a lot of “80s word processor” signs here.

## License

This is under the Unlicense license, so it is in the public domain. Since this isn’t a derivative work, I don’t believe this has enough human involvement to be eligible for copyright. Due to that, and the fact that I don’t really care what people do with this, this is the license chosen.

 * ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * combat_modifiers.c -- The fortified / Sons-of-Liberty / colony-defense
 *   modifier terms of the combat resolver func_05B2C2, reconstructed from
 *   VICEROY.EXE raw bytes.  This file DOCUMENTS the modifier mechanism; it does
 *   NOT re-port the core resolver (see combat.c, already BYTE_VERIFIED).
 *
 * Resolver:  func_05B2C2  @asm file 0x5B2C2..0x5BE30 (reseg page 0x10, ENTER 0x3A,0).
 * Binary:    COLONIZE/VICEROY.EXE
 *            sha256 a17ed64c27671e5e95236e54a7ddc85803a96ba822fbed05e1dad34d3917e2e3
 *
 * ============================================================================
 * HEADLINE FINDING (byte-proven, three independent ways)
 * ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * The single combat ODDS ROLL @0x5B849 uses RAW per-type stat bytes with NO
 * fortify / SoL / colony / terrain multiplier scaling ATK or DEF:
 *
 *     DEF = g_unit_stat[deftype*14 + 0x0B]   (0x523b)   @0x5B823   [V]
 *     ATK = g_unit_stat[atktype*14 + 0x0C]   (0x523c)   @0x5B83B   [V]
 *     total = DEF + ATK                                 @0x5B844   [V]
 *     roll  = random_int(1, total)           (0x181F:0x04D4) @0x5B849 [V]
 *     attacker_wins = (roll <= ATK)                     @0x5B851/0x5B854 [V]
 *
 * Proof 1 — no intervening arithmetic: between the DEF read (0x5B823) and the
 *   ATK read (0x5B83B) and the ADD (0x5B844 `03 C1` = `add ax,cx`) there is no
 *   IMUL / SHL / scaling op on AX or CX. (raw bytes @0x5B819..0x5B846)      [V]
 * Proof 2 — DEF/ATK source never modified: the defender-type local [bp-2] that
 *   indexes DEF is written ONCE (@0x5B2FA =0x10 for "no defender", else @0x5B316
 *   = defender UnitRecord.type), and never re-written by the fort block or any
 *   other path before the roll. (writes to [bp-2] = {0x5B2FA, 0x5B316} only) [V]
 * Proof 3 — table is read nowhere else: across ALL re-segmented overlay pages,
 *   0x523b (DEF) and 0x523c (ATK) are read at EXACTLY three sites, all inside
 *   this roll (page_10.asm lines for 0x5B819/0x5B823/0x5B83B). No other function
 *   reads them with (or without) a multiplier. So a "fortified ATK/DEF scaler"
 *   does not exist anywhere in the overlay image.                            [V]
 *
 * COROLLARY: the long-standing "+50% fortified" hypothesis is REFUTED for this
 * engine. VICEROY combat is base odds = ATK/(ATK+DEF); fortification and colony
 * presence change ROUTING and the post-roll military-strength comparison, not
 * the odds-roll inputs.                                                       [V]
 *
 * ============================================================================
 * WHO REACHES THE ROLL (byte-proven gate)
 * ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * The roll @0x5B849 is reached ONLY through the block at 0x5B7C0, which is
 * entered only when the ATTACKER unit type is a SHIP:
 *     @0x5B7B6  cmp byte[attacker+0x3146], 0x0D ; @0x5B7BB jae 0x5B7C0   (raw: 80 BF 46 31 0D / 73 03) [V]
 *     @0x5B7C0  cmp byte[attacker+0x3146], 0x12 ; @0x5B7C5 jbe 0x5B7CA   (raw: 80 BF 46 31 12 / 76 03) [V]
 *   => attacker type in [0x0D..0x12] (Caravel..Man-O-War) takes the roll; any
 *      other (land) attacker @0x5B7BD `jmp 0x5BAA3` skips it. There is exactly
 *      ONE combat random_int in the whole function (the other RNG @0x5B3B4 is the
 *      ambush 50% coin). (CFG: predecessors of 0x5B819 = {0x5B817} only)       [V]
 *   The roll's DEF input is the DEFENDER's 0x523b; ATK input is the attacking
 *   SHIP's 0x523c.  So this is naval-bombardment / ship-attacks-X odds.        [V]
 *
 * ============================================================================
 * THE FORT BLOCK @0x5B433 — what it really computes (RESOLVED)
 * ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * Reached only when [bp-0x16]!=0, i.e. the ATTACKER is a NON-combatant special
 * unit (type 0xA Treasure / 0 Colonist / 0xC Wagon — set @0x5B331), AND the
 * fort_path flag [bp-0x28]!=0 (a colony/fort is present), AND the defender is a
 * LAND unit (ships 0x0D..0x12 excluded @0x5B414/0x5B41B), AND [bp-2]==0x0F.
 * Then @0x5B451..0x5B497 it computes an ELIGIBILITY THRESHOLD (NOT a stat
 * scale):
 *
 *     def_term = (signed) g_unit_stat[deftype*14 + 0x07]   (0x5237)
 *                          - g_units[def].byte_0x3150;       (UnitRecord +0x0C)   @0x5B471/0x5B477  [V]
 *     atk_term = g_unit_stat[atktype*14 + 0x08]            (0x5238)               @0x5B48F          [V]
 *     if (def_term >= atk_term)  keep [bp-0x24];                                 @0x5B495 cmp / 0x5B497 jge [V]
 *     else                       [bp-0x24] = 0;                                  @0x5B499                  [V]
 *
 *   [bp-0x24] (init 1 @0x5B2D3) is a routing flag consumed @0x5B4B0
 *   (`cmp [bp-0x24],0 / je 0x5B58C`): it decides whether the special unit may
 *   *enter / capture* the fortified colony tile, then runs UI ops
 *   (0x181F:0x812 / 0x894 / 0x844 @0x5B4BC..0x5B4D8). It NEVER feeds the odds
 *   roll. So 0x5237/0x5238 are a colony-capture eligibility pair, not ATK/DEF
 *   modifiers.                                                                  [V]
 *
 * Table provenance: 0x5230-family (stride 14) is the @UNIT record, populated at
 *   game start by the loader @0x74EE0..0x74F59 from NAMES.TXT (each field via
 *   LCALL 0x1A1F:0x88A). Offsets: +0x00 icon(word), +0x06(0x5236) combat-elig,
 *   +0x07(0x5237) and +0x08(0x5238) the colony-capture pair, +0x0B(0x523b) DEF,
 *   +0x0C(0x523c) ATK, +0x0D(0x523d) flag-bits. The exact @UNIT column->field
 *   correspondence for 0x5237/0x5238 (and even for 0x523b/0x523c) is a NAMES.TXT
 *   data question [TBD-data]: the loader @0x74EDA does 12 field-reads (1×0x1A1F:0xB22
 *   + 10×0x1A1F:0x88A + 1×0x1A1F:0xB2E) but each raw @UNIT row has only 11 comma
 *   fields, so the field->offset alignment is NOT a naive 1:1 and must be pinned
 *   from the loader's readers, not the pretty extract. CONFLICT to reconcile:
 *   combat.c's header claims "@UNIT col 3=attack, col 4=defense" map to
 *   0x523b/0x523c, but the loader puts cols 3/4 at 0x5234/0x5236, NOT 0x523b/0x523c.
 *   The ROLL semantics (0x523b=DEF, 0x523c=ATK at the win-threshold) are
 *   byte-certain; the column label is the open item. -> docs/RULINGS.md.   [V/TBD-data]
 *
 * ============================================================================
 * THE REAL MODIFIER LAYER — post-roll military-strength comparison @0x5B85B
 * ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * After the odds roll, the resolver runs a strength-comparison block
 * (@0x5B85B..0x5BA2D) that adjusts attacker_wins ([bp-0x3a]) using PER-POWER
 * military arrays (negative DS offsets, stride 0x13 = 19 bytes per power),
 * the per-type 0x5237 value, and a global scale factor — NOT a fortify% on
 * ATK/DEF. Byte-cited terms:
 *
 *   - per-power x per-type strength: al = [atk_owner*0x13 + (-0x6db4)]   @0x5B889 [V]
 *   - per-power cap:                 cl = [atk_owner + (-0x6d68)]        @0x5B899 [V]
 *     if (al <= cl && [owner-0x6bdc] > 8) ... else attacker_wins=0       @0x5B8A1/0x5B8A3 [V]
 *   - frigate-vs-frigate (type 0x11) special: cmp [def_owner*0x13 - 0x6da3], al  @0x5B8B3..0x5B8CB [V]
 *   - global difficulty scale: al = [atk_owner*0x13 - 0x6da3]; MUL [0x5325]      @0x5B99E/0x5B9A2 [V]
 *   - accumulate: cx -= 0x5237[deftype]; cx -= [def-0x6da4]; ...; [bp-6]=cx       @0x5B9C9..0x5B9DB [V]
 *   - weighted check: ax = lib_weighted(([owner-0x6bf0]>>2), 3, 6) (0x181F:0x35c)
 *                      if (ax > [bp-6]) attacker_wins=1                          @0x5BA0B..0x5BA28 [V]
 *
 *   These per-power arrays (-0x6db4 stride 19, -0x6da4, -0x6da3, -0x6bec,
 *   -0x6be8, -0x6bdc, -0x6bf0, -0x6d68) are the COLONY/POWER military-strength
 *   state (Sons-of-Liberty / veteran / colony-defense bookkeeping lives here,
 *   per the per-power layout). They modify the OUTCOME via comparison, not the
 *   odds-roll inputs. Their precise per-array semantics (which is SoL%, which is
 *   defense bonus) require the per-power init code and are [TBD] beyond this
 *   sub-task's scope; their combat ROLE (post-roll attacker_wins adjustment) is
 *   byte-verified here.                                                          [V/TBD-split]
 *
 * NOTE the global [0x5325] (MUL @0x5B9A2) is a single-byte difficulty/scale
 * factor applied to the per-power strength; not separately xref-indexed.
 * ============================================================================ */
#include "viceroy_types.h"
#include "unit.h"

/* @UNIT per-type record, base DGROUP:0x5230 stride 14. (loader @0x74EE0)  [V] */
extern unsigned char g_unit_stat[];
#define UT_STRIDE          14
#define UT_DEF(t)          (g_unit_stat[(t)*UT_STRIDE + 0x0B])   /* 0x523b  [V] */
#define UT_ATK(t)          (g_unit_stat[(t)*UT_STRIDE + 0x0C])   /* 0x523c  [V] */
#define UT_CAPTURE_D(t)    (g_unit_stat[(t)*UT_STRIDE + 0x07])   /* 0x5237  [V] */
#define UT_CAPTURE_A(t)    (g_unit_stat[(t)*UT_STRIDE + 0x08])   /* 0x5238  [V] */
#define UT_COMBAT_ELIG(t)  (g_unit_stat[(t)*UT_STRIDE + 0x06])   /* 0x5236  [V] */

extern struct UnitRecord g_units[];     /* DGROUP:0x3144 stride 0x1C */
#define U(i)        (g_units[(i)])

/* Per-power military-strength arrays (DGROUP negative offsets, stride 0x13=19
 * per power). LOCAL externs — these are the colony/power-defense state; the
 * resolver reads them ONLY in the post-roll comparison block @0x5B85B..0x5BA2D.
 * Cited by use-site; per-array semantics [TBD beyond combat]. */
extern unsigned char g_pow_strength_by_type[/* power*0x13 + type */];  /* DS:-0x6DB4 @0x5B889 [V] */
extern unsigned char g_pow_strength_cap[/* power */];                  /* DS:-0x6D68 @0x5B899 [V] */
extern unsigned char g_pow_def_term[/* power*0x13 (+...) */];          /* DS:-0x6DA4/-0x6DA3 @0x5B9D5/0x5B99E [V] */
extern unsigned char g_pow_misc_6bec[/* power */];                     /* DS:-0x6BEC @0x5B9A9 [V] */
extern unsigned char g_pow_misc_6be8[/* power */];                     /* DS:-0x6BE8 @0x5B9DE [V] */
extern unsigned char g_pow_count_6bdc[/* power */];                    /* DS:-0x6BDC @0x5B8A3/0x5B9E2 [V] */
extern unsigned char g_pow_misc_6bf0[/* power */];                     /* DS:-0x6BF0 @0x5BA11 [V] */
extern unsigned char g_combat_difficulty_scale;                        /* DS:0x5325  @0x5B9A2 [V] */

/* Library helpers (load-image segment 0x181F; bodies in runtime library,
 * [TBD-libimage]). random_int is the verified one (0x181F:0x04D4). */
extern int  random_int(int lo, int hi);                 /* 0x181F:0x04D4 (rng.c) [V] */
extern int  lib_weighted_pick(int a, int b, int c);     /* 0x181F:0x35C @0x5BA1B [V call] */

/* ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * combat_capture_eligible — the fort block @0x5B433 threshold (documentation
 * mirror; the live code is inside combat_resolve / func_05B2C2 @0x5B451).
 *
 *   Returns nonzero if the special attacker (treasure/colonist/wagon) may take
 *   the fortified colony tile defended by a type-0x0F unit. NOT a stat scaler.
 * @asm 0x5B451..0x5B497                                                     [V] */
int combat_capture_eligible(int attacker_idx, int defender_idx)
{
    int def_type = U(defender_idx).type;                 /* @0x5B457 */
    int atk_type = U(attacker_idx).type;                 /* @0x5B47D */
    /* signed: 0x5237[deftype] - defender.UnitRecord[+0x0C] (struct field
     * cargo_slot_count @0x3150; here used as a dynamic capture-resistance term) */
    int def_term = (int)UT_CAPTURE_D(def_type)
                 - (int)U(defender_idx).cargo_slot_count; /* @0x5B45D/0x5B471..0x5B477 (sub cx,ax) */
    int atk_term = (int)UT_CAPTURE_A(atk_type);           /* @0x5B48F */
    return (def_term >= atk_term);                        /* @0x5B495/0x5B497 jge => eligible */
}

/* ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * combat_ship_odds — the ONE odds roll @0x5B849 (documentation mirror; live in
 * func_05B2C2). Fires only for ship attackers (type 0x0D..0x12). RAW stats.
 * @asm 0x5B819..0x5B854                                                      [V] */
int combat_ship_odds(int attacker_idx, int defender_type)
{
    int def = UT_DEF(defender_type);          /* 0x523b @0x5B823 */
    int atk;
    int total, roll;
    if (def == 0) return 1;                   /* @0x5B819 DEF==0 -> skip combat (return "handled") */
    atk   = UT_ATK(U(attacker_idx).type);     /* 0x523c @0x5B83B (attacker is the ship) */
    total = def + atk;                        /* @0x5B844 (raw sum, NO modifier) */
    roll  = random_int(1, total);             /* @0x5B849 */
    return (roll <= atk);                     /* @0x5B851/0x5B854 attacker(ship) wins iff roll<=ATK */
}

# HEXIS.EXE Reverse Engineering Documentation

## Overview
- **File**: HEXIS.EXE (DOS executable, MZ format)
- **Era**: ~1987-1988
- **Language**: Borland Pascal/Turbo Pascal with BGI graphics
- **Header size**: 0x6f0 (1776 bytes)
- **Code start**: 0x6f0

## Graphics System

### BGI (Borland Graphics Interface)
- **Segment**: 0x0b52
- **Mode**: EGA 640x350 or VGA 640x480 (auto-detect)
- **Font**: Built-in BGI font

### Key BGI Functions (at segment 0x0b52)
| Offset | Function |
|--------|----------|
| 0x036b | InitGraph |
| 0x09ec | SetGraphMode |
| 0x00a3 | GetGraphMode |
| 0x15c6 | SetColor |
| 0x17a5 | SetFillStyle |
| 0x17ed | Bar |
| 0x18e1 | Line |
| 0x0ea4 | MoveTo |
| 0x0ec1 | LineRel |
| 0x0e41 | Line (absolute) |
| 0x11dc | Circle/Arc |
| 0x1a38 | OutTextXY |
| 0x1ac1 | SetTextStyle |
| 0x0520 | RegisterBGIFont |

### Honeycomb Cell Drawing
- Uses LineRel pattern from 0x62b4-0x6370
- Row type 1 (0x62bd-0x62de): LineRel(10, 4), LineRel(19, -8), LineRel(9, 4)
  - Goes: right+down 4px, then right+up 8px, then right+down 4px
  - Creates peak at start, valley in middle, peak at end
- Row type 2 (0x6336-0x6357): LineRel(10, -4), LineRel(19, 8), LineRel(9, -4)
  - Goes: right+up 4px, then right+down 8px, then right+up 4px
  - Creates valley at start, peak in middle, valley at end
- Total wave width: 10 + 19 + 9 = 38px
- Flat segment: 19px (the center part)
- Zigzag amplitude: 8px peak-to-valley (4px up + 4px down from center)
- Row spacing: row * 8 (from shl ax, 3 at 0x6322)
- MoveTo position: (0xe1, row * 8 + 4) = (225, row * 8 + 4)

## Game Variables

### Memory Addresses (Data Segment)
| Address | Size | Description |
|---------|------|-------------|
| 0x6d5 | byte | Action code (keyboard input) |
| 0x6d7 | byte | Piece Y position (row) |
| 0x6d8 | byte | Piece X position (column) |
| 0x6d9 | byte | Piece color |
| 0x6da | byte | Next piece type |
| 0x6db | byte | Current piece type (0-5) |
| 0x6de | word | Score |
| 0x6e0 | byte | Level (1-9) |
| 0x6e3 | byte | Timer counter |
| 0x6ba | byte | Show next piece flag |
| 0x6bb | byte | Sound enabled flag |
| 0x6be | word | GraphDriver |
| 0x6c0 | word | GraphMode |
| 0x34a | array | Board data (26 * rows bytes) |

### Board Layout
- Internal width: 26 (0x1a)
- Board indexing: `(Y * 26 + X)`
- Board array at offset 0x34a from data segment

## Piece System

### Piece Types (6 total)
Piece types 0-5 where types are paired for similar collision behavior:
- Types 0 and 3: Diagonal pieces
- Types 1 and 4: Horizontal pieces
- Types 2 and 5: Horizontal variant pieces

### Rotation Logic (at 0x074bd-0x074ca)
```asm
MOV AL, [0x6db]    ; load current piece type
XOR AH, AH         ; clear high byte
INC AX             ; piece_type + 1
CDQ                ; sign extend for division
MOV CX, 6          ; divisor = 6
IDIV CX            ; AX / 6, remainder in DX
XCHG DX, AX        ; AL = remainder
MOV [0x6db], AL    ; save new piece type
```
**Result**: Rotation = `(piece_type + 1) % 6`, cycling 0→1→2→3→4→5→0

### Piece Cells (from collision code at 0x1a80-0x1c00)
Each piece type has 4 cells calculated relative to anchor (X, Y):

**Type 0/3** (diagonal):
- (X-2, Y-3), (X-1, Y-2), (X, Y-1), (X+1, Y)

**Type 1/4** (horizontal):
- (X-2, Y), (X-1, Y), (X, Y), (X+1, Y)

**Type 2/5** (horizontal variant):
- (X-1, Y), (X, Y), (X+1, Y), (X+2, Y)

## Keyboard Handling

### Key Handler (at 0x07c0-0x08a4)
Reads from port 0x60 (keyboard controller) and sets action code at [0x6d5].

### Scan Codes → Action Mapping
| Scan Code | Key | Action |
|-----------|-----|--------|
| 0x01 | Esc | 2 (restart) |
| 0x02, 0x4f | 1/End | 1 |
| 0x04, 0x51 | 3/PgDn | 3 |
| 0x05, 0x39, 0x4b | 4/Space/Left | 4 (drop) |
| 0x07, 0x4d | 6/Right | 6 (level up) |
| 0x08, 0x47 | 7/Home | 7 (move left) |
| 0x09, 0x48 | 8/Up | 8 (rotate) |
| 0x0a, 0x49 | 9/PgUp | 9 (move right) |
| 0x44 | F10 | Boss key |

### Action Codes
| Code | Action |
|------|--------|
| 1 | Toggle next piece preview |
| 2 | Restart game |
| 3 | Toggle sound |
| 4 | Hard drop |
| 6 | Increase level |
| 7 | Move left |
| 8 | Rotate (cycle piece type) |
| 9 | Move right |

## Collision Detection (0x1a80-0x1c00)

Checks if piece can move to new position by:
1. Loading piece type from [0x6db]
2. Checking piece type (0/3, 1/4, or 2/5)
3. For each cell offset, checking board[Y*26+X+offset] == 0

## Scoring System

### Strings
- "Score : 0" at 0x6fc7
- "+1000" bonus string nearby
- "Full Lines" at 0x6fb8
- "Top Twenty" at 0x700e

### Score Increment Patterns
Found at various locations:
- Base score per line: 100
- Bonus for multiple lines: +1000 (4 lines), +300 (3 lines), +100 (2 lines)
- Score multiplied by level

## Line Clearing

- Check horizontal rows for completion
- Full row = all cells non-zero
- Pattern at [0x34a + Y*26 + X] checked for each X in row
- CMP byte ptr [di + 0x34a], 0 in loops

## Game Loop

### Timer
- INT 1Ah used for timing
- Timer counter at [0x6e3]
- Pieces fall faster at higher levels

### Main Loop
1. Handle keyboard input → set action code
2. Process action (move/rotate/drop)
3. Check collisions
4. Lock piece if can't move
5. Clear completed lines
6. Spawn next piece
7. Update score/display
8. Repeat

## EGA Colors (0-15)
| Index | Color |
|-------|-------|
| 0 | Black |
| 1 | Blue |
| 2 | Green |
| 3 | Cyan |
| 4 | Red |
| 5 | Magenta |
| 6 | Brown |
| 7 | Light Gray |
| 8 | Dark Gray |
| 9 | Light Blue |
| 10 | Light Green |
| 11 | Light Cyan |
| 12 | Light Red |
| 13 | Light Magenta |
| 14 | Yellow |
| 15 | White |

## Screen Layout

### Coordinates (from analysis)
- Board starts at X = 0xe1 (225)
- Board area uses ~11 columns, ~21 rows
- Next piece preview on right side
- Score/level info on left side (X < 225)

### Key Positions
- "Play HEXIS !" title: top center
- Level selection: center screen
- Score display: left side
- Hot keys help: right side

; DEMON0.RDF - "Demon World", the colony on Pollux V where the landing
; party beams down. Prelate Angiven walks out to meet them; the doors of
; the two buildings open when the crew walks to them.
;
; Actors: 8 Prelate Angiven, 9 the right door, 10 (0Ah) the left door.
; Objects: 20h the buildings, 21h/22h the trees, 23h the snow, 24h the
; bushes, 25h the sign, 26h/27h the ground in front of the left/right door.
; Regions 0/1: the doorsteps. Exit 0: the path to the mountain.
;
; Labels: H_ script headers, L branch targets, C_ conversations,
; T_/N_/S_ strings; talk_buf: the conversation buffer of Say.
;
; Quirks of the original:
; - The script chain runs on into code at 0838: the engine reads its bytes
;   as key 50 B8 03 00 and next 2E50 (beyond rdf_scripts_end, so the search
;   stops).

	INCLUDE	rdf.inc

; RoomState.vars, shared by the mission's rooms (cleared by StartAway)
was_rude	EQU	RS_VARS+0	; word: lost points for doubting the Prelate
met_prelate	EQU	RS_VARS+0Ah	; talked to the Prelate
prelate_greeted	EQU	RS_VARS+0Ch	; he has said hello
asked_witnesses	EQU	RS_VARS+0Dh	; asked to see the witnesses
flora_said	EQU	RS_VARS+0Fh	; McCoy has remarked on the plants
came_from	EQU	RS_VARS+11h	; 1: from the colony, 2: from the mine; which way the crew face
score	EQU	RS_VARS+2Fh	; word: the mission's score

RDF	SEGMENT BYTE PUBLIC 'RDF'
	ASSUME	CS:RDF, DS:NOTHING, ES:NOTHING, SS:NOTHING

rdf_service	LABEL	BYTE
	DD	0	; ScriptService, set by LoadRoom
rdf_state	LABEL	BYTE
	DW	0	; &room, set by LoadRoom
rdf_y_max	LABEL	BYTE
	DW	0BFh	; depth scaling: y range
rdf_y_min	LABEL	BYTE
	DW	6Eh
rdf_scale_min	LABEL	BYTE
	DW	32h	; and scale range
rdf_scale_max	LABEL	BYTE
	DW	100h
rdf_sections	LABEL	BYTE
	DW	OFFSET rdf_scripts, OFFSET rdf_scripts_end	; scripts, objects, exits, regions, bans: start, end
	DW	OFFSET rdf_objects, OFFSET rdf_objects_end
	DW	OFFSET rdf_exits, OFFSET rdf_exits_end
	DW	OFFSET rdf_regions, OFFSET rdf_regions_end
	DW	OFFSET rdf_bans, OFFSET rdf_bans_end
rdf_exit_room	LABEL	BYTE
	DW	1, 5, 6, -1	; room for each exit
rdf_walk_in	LABEL	BYTE
				; per entrance, for each crew member: from, to
	DW	60,114, 86,158	; entrance 0, crew 0
	DW	60,114, 66,153	; entrance 0, crew 1
	DW	60,114, 106,147	; entrance 0, crew 2
	DW	60,114, 80,140	; entrance 0, crew 3
	DW	250,162, 99,172	; entrance 1, crew 0
	DW	250,162, 128,171	; entrance 1, crew 1
	DW	250,162, 146,176	; entrance 1, crew 2
	DW	250,162, 177,170	; entrance 1, crew 3
	DW	157,134, 78,155	; entrance 2, crew 0
	DW	157,134, 64,146	; entrance 2, crew 1
	DW	157,134, 98,155	; entrance 2, crew 2
	DW	157,134, 86,139	; entrance 2, crew 3
	DW	0,0, 0,0	; entrance 3, crew 0
	DW	0,0, 0,0	; entrance 3, crew 1
	DW	0,0, 0,0	; entrance 3, crew 2
	DW	0,0, 0,0	; entrance 3, crew 3
rdf_beam_pos	LABEL	BYTE
	DW	86,158, 66,153, 106,147, 80,140	; beaming in
rdf_stand_pos	LABEL	BYTE
	DW	0,0, 0,0, 0,0, 0,0
; In the room file, so these start at 0 each time the room loads
right_door_steps	LABEL	BYTE
	DB	0
left_door_steps	LABEL	BYTE
	DB	0
going_left_door	LABEL	BYTE
	DB	0
going_right_door	LABEL	BYTE
	DB	0
N_prelclap	LABEL	BYTE
	DB	'prelclap',0
N_prel	LABEL	BYTE
	DB	'prel',0
N_s0r0d1	LABEL	BYTE
	DB	's0r0d1',0
N_s0r0d3	LABEL	BYTE
	DB	's0r0d3',0
N_s0r0d2	LABEL	BYTE
	DB	's0r0d2',0
N_s0r0d4	LABEL	BYTE
	DB	's0r0d4',0
	DB	'skille',0
N_sscans	LABEL	BYTE
	DB	'sscans',0
N_mscans	LABEL	BYTE
	DB	'mscans',0

rdf_scripts:
; The room starts: wind, and the closed doors.
H_010D:
	SCRIPT	MSG_TICK, 1, 0, 0, H_015C
StartRoom:
	jmp	SHORT L011E

N_DEM0LOOP	LABEL	BYTE
	DB	'DEM0LOOP',0
L011E:
	push	OFFSET N_DEM0LOOP
	mov	ax, RC_SFX
	push	ax
	SERVICE		; Sfx("DEM0LOOP")
	add	sp, 4
	push	0
	push	99h
	push	0FCh
	push	OFFSET N_s0r0d3
	push	9
	push	RC_ANIM0
	SERVICE		; Anim0(9, "s0r0d3", 252, 153, 0)
	add	sp, 0Ch
	push	0
	push	82h
	push	9Eh
	push	OFFSET N_s0r0d4
	push	0Ah
	push	RC_ANIM0
	SERVICE		; Anim0(10, "s0r0d4", 158, 130, 0)
	add	sp, 0Ch
	retf

; The Prelate walks out to meet the landing party...
H_015C:

sources.reason: Native .NET/MonoGame game logic with recovered story state, original resource readers and text read from supported DOS executable as data. Inspected persisted story-progress bitfield controller.
Native .NET/raylib game session and interaction dispatcher, with original packed graphics and TFMX playback replacing Amiga host hardware.
Reverse-engineered MiamiDx external library/driver ABI implemented over a new protocol core. Inspected LVO/interface research and native bsdsocket implementation.
Recovered DOS/4GW game C/assembly with DOS and Windows address annotations and reproducible comparison tools. Inspected economy/formula source and current build configuration.

Named TASM reconstruction plus structured C combat/game regions and separate native SDL3 backend. Source-generated image is inert state data; original offset identities dispatch to named C services, not CPU execution.

Recovered procedural Pascal plus compiler probes, original-format mapping and behavioral tests. Upstream claims all 47200 bytes and 787 ordered relocations match with no oracle linkage or post-build patch.

Native document-carrier parsing/editing core grounded in controlled DOS observations and binary evidence. Inspected word navigation and bounded compatibility profiles rather than relying on a lookalike UI.
Recovered LORD 4.07 game/configuration sources and backwards version patches reaching 1.7; inspected native bank routines.
VICEROY executable/RTLink overlay analysis, byte-addressed formula studies and partial C reconstruction. Inspected combat-modifier evidence and corrective audit.
Full disassembly-derived EGAME assembly skeleton plus progressive MSC 5.1 C replacements; inspected combat code and detailed differential-test status.
Recovered BASRUN-hosted game logic and fixed-record world data mapped into native Python. End-of-turn module links behavior to executable routine 0x269e.
Substantive loader, ByteKiller, memory-image and copper/framebuffer research with reproducible scripts and Ghidra function map.
Original BIN/ILN resource formats decoded into a Godot lab prototype. Inspected native archive reader handles offset wrapping, palette chunks and RLE rather than running DOS code.
Recovered CD-release engine and separate native machine-code RDF room scripts; inspected bridge C and annotated Demon World assembly.
Recovered game functions, library identification and original-link reconstruction; inspected native bridge module and detailed mismatch ledger.
Recovered board/input/BGI analysis and actual Pascal plus Python game sources, beyond the bundled original.
Native Nintendo 64 remake of DOS Vlak, but reviewed README/tree does not establish binary-derived source or algorithm recovery. Keep as port lead rather than assert reverse engineering.
Reverse-engineered Amiga demos, not games/applications in this focused request. Useful separately scoped demo batch, not rejected for quality.
Modern Linux benchmark inspired by SYSTEM SPEED TEST; reviewed evidence does not establish original algorithm recovery or comparable historical scoring. No raw-device benchmark executed.
README explicitly says repository contains built static output only, with data embedded in Wasm. Source reconstruction exists elsewhere but is not reviewable here.
Substantial matching demo reconstruction but outside game/application focus. Preserve caveat that DemoVT is copied, not rebuilt, and two original debug tails are excluded from comparison.
Small high-refresh patch package pointing to neuromancer/wc1-re; not an independent complete source recovery. Original authority is Windows Kilrathi Saga with partial DOS data compatibility.
Delphi 3 Windows game, not DOS despite packed-DOS-date resource metadata. Upstream also reports 221 remaining resource bytes different; not full-file identical.
Early Windows WinText format recovery and converters, not a DOS application. Retain for Windows document-format research without widening this pass.

Useful historical lineage/archive with preserved Unix C reader, but its relation to original DOS TODAY source is unresolved. Browser recreation lives separately; do not label the root recovered DOS source.
